free_tier.stated: The fund's own post describes 'a minimum $1K stipend' and 'offering smaller $1K grants to young people to help nudge them to build'; it calls the award 'a no strings attached grant — we don't own you, your project, any IP generated, future equity in anything you generate, etc. It's a Venmo payment.' The published route is an email to any partner at the fund with 'a five minute Loom video'. Eligibility is by career stage, not by institution: '1517 Medici Project works with high school, college students, and dropouts'. The geographic limit is stated on the same page.

chaining: Nothing composes outside North America: the award is USD 1,000 by Venmo, which is both too small to matter and unreachable from the wrong country. Inside North America it would be a genuine no-strings USD 1,000 with the widest IP terms in this class.

limits.value: the payment rail fails before anything else: the fund states in its own post that it cannot issue grants to teams based outside North America, so a team based elsewhere is excluded regardless of project quality, and the amount is only about USD 1,000 even when it does pay.

notes: A REFUTATION of the shape rather than of the programme: this is the cleanest illustration in the class that 'no strings attached' and 'anywhere in the world' are separate claims, and that the payment rail is the one that decides reachability. The fund is candid about it, which is why the record can be documented rather than inferred. The corpus should keep this row because the terms are otherwise the best in the class (explicitly no IP claim, no equity, no reporting, no application form) and because a reader who sees 'no strings attached grants of USD 1,000' in an aggregator will otherwise apply from the wrong country and lose a month. Note the parent fund's own page does not state an upper bound and describes the award as a minimum, so 'at least USD 1,000' is the correct reading; no published example of a larger Medici award was found.
